bib.title: The Efficiency Spectrum of Large Language Models: An Algorithmic Survey

read.skipped: Reference list read to entry [140] in full; remainder (entries 141-352) skimmed only for lineage, not read line by line.

question: What algorithmic techniques make LLMs more efficient across the whole development pipeline: scaling laws, data, architecture, training and tuning, and inference?
contributions: A holistic algorithmic survey of LLM efficiency covering budget (scaling laws), data, architecture, training and tuning, and inference, in contrast to surveys on a single area
Defines efficiency as optimizing computational and memory resources without compromising model performance
Covers research mostly before September 2023 plus selected later work; hardware advances are omitted

results.claim: Kaplan et al. fit test loss against dataset size as a power law with exponent 0.095.
results.setup: Transformer language models; loss L as a function of dataset size D
results.note: Equation is garbled by extraction: printed as L(D) ≈ (5.4 x 10^13 / D)^0.095.

results.claim: Chinchilla (70B parameters) outperformed the 280B Gopher at a similar compute budget.
results.setup: Compute-optimal training under scaling law L(N, D); Gopher as the larger baseline
results.quote: Chinchilla, with 70 billion parameters, which outperformed the larger 280 billion parameter Gopher model

results.claim: In the data-constrained regime, up to 4 epochs of repeated data change the loss negligibly versus one epoch at fixed compute.
results.setup: Fixed compute budget, limited training data
results.quote: training with up to 4 epochs of repeated data yields
results.note: More epochs than 4 reduce performance, per the survey.

results.claim: Redesigned architectures reach similar downstream fine-tuning quality to T5-base with 50% fewer parameters and 40% faster training.
LLMs can be pruned unstructured to at least 50% sparsity one-shot at minimal accuracy loss, but real speedup needs specialised software or hardware.
results.source: unstructured pruning works cited in Sec 7.2 (e.g. [117], [242])
results.setup: LLMs, with or without retraining; larger LLMs more compressible
results.quote: LLMs can be pruned to at least 50% sparsity in one-shot

results.claim: NVIDIA 2:4 semi-structured sparsity prunes two of every four weights (50% sparse) and is accelerated on Ampere GPUs; other N:M ratios are not accelerated.
results.setup: A100-class Ampere Tensor Core GPUs at inference
results.quote: For every contiguous array of four weights, two are pruned, yielding a 50%-sparse net.
results.note: 2:4 appears in text as the proposed scheme.

results.claim: Adapter tuning adds inference latency of roughly 4-6% because it changes the computational graph.
results.setup: Serial adapters added to transformer layers

results.claim: GLaM activates only 99 billion of over 1.2 trillion parameters at inference through mixture of experts.
Model parameter counts grow about 410x every two years while GPU memory grew only 5x (16GB to 80GB).
results.setup: Large transformer models vs GPU memory, no citation given at the sentence
results.quote: increasing by approximately 410× every two years

results.claim: Activation compressed training (2-bit average) allows batch sizes 6.6x to 14x larger.
results.setup: Compressing saved activations to average 2 bits across multiple tasks
results.quote: ranging from 6.6× to 14× larger than traditional methods

results.claim: BPipe speeds up training of GPT-3 96B and 134B by 1.25 to 2.17 times versus Megatron-LM.
Fine-tuning only the last few layers reaches up to 90% of the performance of full fine-tuning.
results.setup: Partial parameter tuning of final layers
results.quote: achieving up to 90% of the performance of a fully fine-tuned model

results.claim: Standard warm-up cosine LR practice: warm-up over 0.1-0.5% of steps then decay to about 10% of peak; PaLM grew batch from 1M to 4M tokens.
results.quote: typically 0.1% to 0.5% of total training steps

results.claim: Attention-free methods (RWKV, RetNet, Mamba) have O(1) per-token inference time and O(n) memory versus O(n^2) memory for the Transformer; RetNet and Mamba rated +++ performance.
results.setup: Sequence length n; qualitative performance rating from perplexity
results.table: Table 1, rows Transformer, RWKV, H3, Hyena, RetNet, Mamba, columns Time Cost, Memory Cost, Performance
results.note: Qualitative table (plus signs), no measured value.

results.claim: Quantization is currently more popular and mature than structured pruning for LLM compression; structured pruning of LLMs is early-stage.
results.setup: LLM compression, because retraining data and compute are unavailable

limits: Survey covers works mostly before September 2023 plus selected later work; footnote 1 concedes relevant studies may be missed.
Hardware advances are omitted by design (footnote 2).
No experiments of its own; every number is quoted from cited work and mostly without setup.

Inference section covers only compression (pruning, distillation, quantization, low-rank); it has no coverage of speculative decoding, KV-cache management, batching or serving. PagedAttention and FlashDecoding appear briefly under attention.
Authors say structured pruning of LLMs is early stage and that choosing curriculum difficulty metrics and pacing needs task-specific experiments.
Quantization section gives no bit-width or accuracy numbers.
practices: Prefer post-training quantization over quantization-aware training for LLMs because retraining cost and data access are prohibitive (Sec 7.4).
Use the 2:4 sparsity pattern when targeting NVIDIA Ampere GPUs, since unstructured sparsity rarely gives real speedup without specialised support (Sec 7.2).
Use FlashAttention and PagedAttention-style IO-aware and paged KV management to cut memory traffic and fragmentation (Sec 5.2).
Use warm-up plus cosine LR decay, AdamW or Adafactor, gradient clipping, and restart from checkpoint on loss spikes for stable pretraining (Sec 6.2.1).
Use BF16 over FP16 mixed precision for more reliable training (Sec 6.2.2).
Use ZeRO partitioning and offload to cut data-parallel memory redundancy (Sec 6.2.4).
Use parameter-efficient tuning such as LoRA or QLoRA instead of full fine-tuning (Sec 6.3).
Use scaling laws to choose model size and data under a fixed compute budget (Sec 3.2).
